newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Reports find Asian mini-states are top economies.
newsitem.headline: Reports find Asian mini-states are top economies.

text.p: Asian mini-states Singapore and Hong Kong are maintaining their challenge to the United States in the global economic competitiveness league, according to two rival Swiss reports issued this week.

Both annual reports, based on a wide range of business surveys and statistics, also found Britain, Ireland, Canada and Netherlands bounding up the table in reflection of the effect of policies based on privatisation and deregulation.

But they were at odds over the performance of such widely differing economies as Finland, a relatively new member of the European Union, of Indonesia, and of China -- which one found moving up strongly and the other saw slipping back.

The reports are issued by the Geneva-based World Economic Forum and the Lausanne International Institute for Management Development (IMD) -- which worked together on the annual project for six years but split up from the end of 1995.

The Forum, organiser of the yearly gathering of world political and business leaders in the Swiss mountain report of Davos, found Singapore and Hong Kong the global numbers one and two in competitiveness for the second year in succession.

Its report put the United States in third place, one up on last year when New Zealand occupied this position. New Zealand, according to the Forum, slipped back to fifth place, overtaken also by Canada which was only eighth in 1996.

But the IMD set the United States at the top of its table followed by Singapore and Hong Kong, as it had last year, with Finland up from 15th to fourth, Norway at fifth against sixth in 1996, and the Netherlands sixth, also one place higher.

The Forum, which defines competitivess as "the ability of a country to achieve sustained high rates of growth in GDP (gross domestic product) per capita", calls its study the "Global Competitiveness Report."

Co-chairman of the advisory board for compilation of the 140-page document and Harvard economics professor Jeffrey Sachs argues that competitive nations "are the ones that have chosen the institutions and policies that promote long-term growth."

The IMD, a renowned management school which maintains a special research team headed by economics professor Stephane Garelli who also teaches at Lausanne University, terms its publication "The World Competitiveness Yearbook."

Garelli says the Yearbook -- which the IMD also makes available on the Internet and is to be updated throughout the year -- "ranks and assesses how a nation's environment sustains value-added creation."

Both publications use eight overall factors to determine competitiveness. Between 1990 and 1995, the joint report was widely used by global companies and financial corporations to provide guidance in investment decisions.

But some businessmen and analysts say the rivalry between the two institutions, which leads to both apparently trying to outsmart each other in publicising their findings first, has reduced the reports' value.

"The gross variance in the assessment of some key countries has just highlighted for many of us the precarious nature of what must be after all a rather subjective exercise," said one Geneva-based executive.

The Forum said Singapore and Hong Kong "excel in nearly every major area that counts in terms of competitiveness", citing "open financial markets, corruption-free civil service, superb infrastructure and highly-educated labour force."

The IMD hailed the United States for a "remarkable and consistent performance" which made it more competitive than ever, but warned that U.S. workers could start pressing for better rewards after years of wage stagnation.

The Forum put Canada on fourth place "thanks to its success in curbing its fiscal deficit", against eighth last year, while the IMD set it in 10th place against 12th last year, suggesting it was helped by proximity to the buoyant U.S. economy.

Britain was hailed by the Forum, which moved it from 15th last year to seventh, for a "dramatic improvement". The IMD said it had climbed from 19th to 11th on their table because of "robust economic growth" and declining unemployment.

Germany was down to 14th from 10th last year in the IMD league and from 23rd to 25th in the Forum rating, while France climbed just one place from 20th to 19th according to the IMD and remained stuck at 23rd.

Both surveys blamed the poor performance of the two major EU powers on fiscal and labour market policies, which the Forum said had caused a "chronic crisis in declining competitiveness" across much of the 15-member EU.

The IMD put China at 27th against 26th last year, while the Forum moved it up from 36th to 29th. In another major variance, the Forum promoted Indonesia from 30th to 15th, while the IMD rating for the Asian "new tiger" was 39th against 41st in 1996.
